reading.body:
Authors Guild v. HathiTrust, a 2014 case holding that digitizing a library of books for full-text search and print-disabled access was fair use, is the cleanest authority in this collection for the claim that copying a complete corpus can be lawful without any output of the original expression being required.

It sits alongside Sega, Kelly, and Google v. Oracle in the same broad 79-case defense pool, but its own stated limit is unusually direct. HathiTrust's system returned page numbers rather than text, and a generative model that can emit passages resembling the originals is not obviously on the same side of that line, which is a narrower gap between precedent and current practice than some of the other cases in this set.

The data does not say how courts have treated that gap in the citing cases specifically, only that the case itself draws the line at returning locations rather than content.
